### Saved approvals

When OpenCode asks, "Always allow" saves the pattern `*` for that tool's action, for every path in the case of an
export. The saved answer applies to every agent in the OpenCode project, Plan included, until you remove it. See
[SECURITY.md](../SECURITY.md).

### Runs where nobody is present

In `opencode run`, schedules and other runs where nobody can answer a prompt, a call that would ask is refused as
needing approval, and the tool does not run. Granola's reads still work. To let such a run make a change
or write an export, allow that tool with a rule, as in the recipes above.

`opencode run --auto` approves every request that no rule denies, Granola's writes included. Prefer rules for the
tools you need.

## Errors

Every error has a code, a message and a next step, in the form `CODE: message Next step: next step`.

### Connection and setup

| Code | Message | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `NOT_REGISTERED` | The Granola connection isn't registered yet. | Retry in a few seconds; if it persists, check that no organisation policy (mcp.use) or other plugin removes the granola server, then restart OpenCode. |
| `CONNECTING` | Granola is still connecting. | Retry in a few seconds. |
| `AUTH_REQUIRED` | Granola needs you to sign in. | Run /connect and choose Granola, then press o or Enter to open the sign-in page (in a terminal, opencode mcp auth granola opens it automatically). |
| `CONNECTION_FAILED` | Granola connection failed: *reason*, ending with one full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. | Reconnect Granola from /mcps, and if it keeps failing, run /connect and choose Granola to sign in again. |
| `DISABLED` | Granola is disabled in OpenCode. | Enable granola in /mcps, or remove "disabled": true from mcp.servers.granola in your OpenCode config. |
| `TOOL_UNAVAILABLE` | Granola does not offer *tool* for this account. | Your Granola plan may not include it; run /granola-status to see the tools Granola offers you. |
| `HOST_UNTESTED` | The Granola plugin supports OpenCode >=2.2.3 <2.4.0, found *version*. | Use OpenCode >=2.2.3 <2.4.0, or set the plugin option allowUntestedHost to true to run anyway. |
| `OPTIONS_INVALID` | Plugin option *key* *problem*. | Fix the Granola plugin options in your OpenCode config, then reload OpenCode. |
| `STATUS_UNAVAILABLE` | Granola status could not be read. | Run /granola-status again in a few seconds. The status RPC answers with its error `unavailable`, and the `/granola` dialog says to press r in a few seconds. |
| `SKILLS_INVALID` | The bundled skill *path* needs front matter with a name that matches its folder and a description. | Reinstall the plugin. |
| `PACKAGE_INVALID` | The Granola plugin's package.json *problem*. | Reinstall the plugin. |

Scripts that use the tools RPC get their own error codes; see [Scripting](scripting.md#errors).

When a Granola tool fails because the server is not available, the plugin replaces OpenCode's message with the
matching connection error. The reason in `CONNECTION_FAILED` is shortened to one line, with web addresses
replaced by `<url>`. OpenCode's sign-in error is never repeated, because it can contain a sign-in link.

# In Jelly

[Jelly](https://heyjelly.ai) runs OpenCode agents. It reads the `jelly` section of this
package's `package.json` as JSON, without loading the plugin, when a person reviews the exact
version, and uses it as follows.

Jelly names the plugin **Granola** (`jelly.title`), with the package name and version beneath. Under
that name it shows the one line in `jelly.summary`, and beside it the mark in `jelly.icon`
(`assets/icon.svg`, shipped in the package): Jelly reads that file once, when it records the
plugin, and keeps it only if it is a clean SVG of drawing elements, with no script, style, link
or outside reference. A Jelly whose declaration schema lacks `summary` or `icon` refuses this
declaration, because that schema accepts no unknown keys.

## Tools and permissions

21 tools are declared (11 read-only). Jelly's agents have no base "allow everything"
rule, so this plugin's own default rules, which it puts after that rule, never reach them. Jelly
writes each declared `ask` or `deny` as that tool's default instead (the person's own choice
replaces it), and denies a read-only helper every tool not marked `readOnly`. A declared `allow`
changes nothing in Jelly.

- Ask: none. Every tool is allowed by default, in Jelly as in OpenCode.
- Off: none.
- Everything else runs, as the plugin's own rules let it. That includes `granola_give_feedback`, which sends a report to
  Granola's team and which Granola's own instructions tell the model to send unasked, and
  `granola_export_markdown`, which writes a file outside the project. A Jelly admin turns either into an ask, or off,
  in Jelly's own tool settings; in OpenCode the same is a rule, or the `access` option. `granola_events_list` is the plugin's own read for Memory's collector, which runs it unattended, so it never asks; its `probe`, a tools RPC method rather than a tool, is not declared here.

`granola_sign_out` is declared, not read-only, with a note: Granola serves it as a destructive change (it revokes the
sign-in for every connection that shares it), so a read-only helper is never given it. The plugin removes it from the
agents' tools in OpenCode and in Jelly alike; sign out from the card, or with `opencode mcp logout granola`.
`granola_create_meeting_note_from_transcript` is one of Granola's writes: it creates a private note.

A tool the upstream server adds later is not declared, so in Jelly it is not asked about by
default. Keep `jelly.tools` in step with the known-tool list; `test/jelly.test.ts` checks
each declared effect against the plugin's own default rules, and the list against the known tools.
`test/live-tools.test.ts` checks the declaration against Granola's own tool list, captured live on 14 November 2026
in `test/fixtures/live-tools.json` (`provenance.json` says how): every tool Granola serves is declared, every declared
tool is served or is the plugin's own (`test/fixtures/tool-registry.json`), and each `readOnly` is Granola's
`readOnlyHint`.

Declared: `granola`, `granola-meeting-brief`. Jelly refuses an install whose

## Signing in

`jelly.signIns` declares one sign-in, `granola`, for Granola's MCP server `granola`, which signs in with OpenCode's MCP OAuth. When the server needs a new sign-in, the row says Sign in again. OpenCode can keep reporting a server whose token was turned down mid-session as connected until it connects again; Jelly has the engine reconnect it when a call fails that way.

Jelly folds the declared sign-ins into this plugin's one card, which shows each as Connected, Not signed in or Sign in again (expired or revoked), and starts, renews and signs out of each. An agent's `jelly_connection_request`, or a tool result that names this plugin's "Run /connect and choose …" next step, opens the same card. The plugin still signs in through OpenCode, as it does without Jelly; the declaration only tells Jelly which of the engine's integrations and servers are this plugin's.

## Settings

`jelly.contributes.settings` declares one setting, `access`, the option of the same name, as a choice of three:
**Allowed** (`all`, the default), **Ask before changes** (`ask-changes`) and **Read only** (`read-only`), with Jelly's
own line for each. Jelly draws it as a choice, never as free text, and saves only one of the three. A Jelly that does
not know declared choices yet refuses the whole declaration, so this needs a Jelly that does.

`exportDirectory`, an absolute path, and `allowUntestedHost` are not declared: they are set in `opencode.json`.

## Versions

Jelly's curated catalogue pins an exact version. Each release is published under a new version, so a review in
Jelly can tell the two apart.

The declaration test runs the shared kit, `test/support/jelly-kit.ts`, which checks the declaration and this page against Jelly's plugin authors' standard. `scripts/check-copies.mjs` holds the kit equal to the copy every plugin carries. The tools RPC and the source contract come from the pinned `@we-the-rebel-alliance/source-contract` package, bundled into `dist/index.js`; `package.json`'s `sources` declares `granola.meetings`, which Jelly reads from the installed package.

# Scripting

A script can call every Granola tool this plugin knows with no model: a cron job, a shell script, or any program that
can reach the OpenCode server. It uses the tools RPC, `granola.meetings.tools`, through `opencode api` or an OpenCode
client.

| Method | The tool | Class |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `get_account_info`, `list_meeting_folders`, `search_meetings`, `get_meetings`, `get_meeting_transcript`, `query_granola_meetings`, `get_meeting_attachment`, `list_templates`, `search_transcripts`, `get_agent_brief` | the ten reads | read |
| `create_folder`, `update_folder`, `add_note_to_folder`, `remove_note_from_folder`, `update_private_notes`, `generate_summary`, `create_meeting_note_from_transcript` | Granola's writes | write |
| `give_feedback` | sends to Granola's team | send |
| `export_markdown` | the plugin's export: writes a Markdown file under the export folder | export |
| `events_list`, `probe` | the plugin's own reads, the `granola.meetings` source: the meetings you took part in as events, and who is signed in ([Events list](configuration.md#events-list)) | read |
| `describe` | none: lists the methods, their classes, permission actions, whether OpenCode lists each tool now, and each tool's input as JSON Schema | – |

The class is the worst thing a tool can do. It never decides whether a call runs: the rules do, and at the default
`access` every method is allowed.

Each method runs Granola's own tool with the same input, through OpenCode's own connection and sign-in. The plugin
never sees the token. Granola decides which tools an account gets: on the free plan, for example, the transcript and
folder tools fail or are not listed.

`sign_out` is not a method: it is not a tool this plugin offers (the plugin removes it), and `opencode mcp logout
granola` is the way to revoke the grant. A tool Granola adds later is not a method until it is classified;
`describe` lists it as unclassified.

## A script runs as a session

Every call names a session, and the session must name an agent. Create it for the script once, with the agent the script
runs as, and keep its id (`data.id` in the reply). Give the project as the session's `location`: a session made without one belongs to the service's default location, where the project's agents may not exist, and each call then fails `Agent not found`. For example:

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"weekly meetings","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"}}'
```

Never borrow a session found through history or a list: the script would run as that session's agent, under its rules.
The script then runs as that agent, with exactly the access its model would have:

- The call resolves the tool's action, such as `granola_get_meetings`, against the agent's rules and then the
  session's, with the host's order (the last matching rule wins). Only an `allow` runs.
- **A script gets the same default as the model: every tool is allowed.** At the default `access: "all"`, the plugin's
  block allows every known tool and the `granola_*` namespace, so a script can read, write, send and export. To restrict
  a script, set the plugin option `"access": "ask-changes"` (an ask is refused, because no one can answer a prompt for a
  script) or `"access": "read-only"` (everything but the reads is denied), or give the script's agent or session a later
  rule. An `ask` and a `deny` are refused, with no tool call and no prompt left waiting; OpenCode's own executor then
  checks the call again, as it does for the model. An agent defined only in your config gets no default rules;
  `/granola-status` names it and gives the fix.
- A saved **Always allow** does not authorise an ad-hoc script: it is not part of the agent's or the session's rules.
  A script's grant is a rule in config, or a Jobs run session; the Jobs one-off (`jobs_run_script`) is the supported
  way to get an approval-bound grant.

Session rules come after the agent's, so a session can narrow what its script may do. This one can list and read
meetings, but not read transcripts or ask questions across meetings:

```sh
opencode api post /api/session -d '{"title":"weekly meetings","agent":"build","location":{"directory":"/path/to/project"},"permissions":[
  {"action":"granola_*","resource":"*","effect":"deny"},
  {"action":"granola_search_meetings","resource":"*","effect":"allow"},
  {"action":"granola_get_meetings","resource":"*","effect":"allow"}
]}'
```

## Calling a method

The body is `{"input": {"sessionID": "<session>", "input": <the tool's input>}}`. Both keys are required, and no other
key is allowed:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/granola.meetings.tools/search_meetings -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…","input":{"limit":10}}}'
```

The tool's input is Granola's: `describe` shows each tool's schema as OpenCode lists it now. Check it rather than guess a
field name.

`describe` takes nothing, or a session to resolve each method's permission for:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/granola.meetings.tools/describe -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{}}'
opencode api post /api/rpc/granola.meetings.tools/describe -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…"}}'
```

The plugin's own export takes the fields its schema gives; a transcript export of one meeting, into a named file, is:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/granola.meetings.tools/export_markdown -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{"input":{"sessionID":"ses_…","input":{"meeting_ids":["m-1"],"content":"transcript","path":"meetings/m-1.md"}}}'
```

## The location

Run the command in the project whose agent you mean, and send the call to that location explicitly:

```sh
opencode api post /api/rpc/granola.meetings.tools/<method> -H "x-opencode-directory:$PWD" -d '{…}'
```

Without it the call goes to the service's default location and fails `rpc.unavailable` if the plugin is not loaded
there. The HTTP equivalents are the `location[directory]` query parameter and the same header. `describe` reports the
`location` that answered and a `locationHint`.

A location unloads after OpenCode's idle timeout. If a scheduled script gets `rpc.unavailable` from a location that was
loaded before, send the call again once: the request loads the location. Jobs keeps its own location loaded.

## Results

A result comes back as `{ output?, text }`: the tool's structured content when it has any, and its text parts joined by
newlines. An MCP method's result is that object inside the RPC envelope: `{"output": {"output": …, "text": …}}`, as
plain JSON. An `export_markdown` result is the file's `path`, `bytes` and `sha256`, with a short summary in `text`.

Meeting content in it is untrusted: notes, transcripts and titles hold what other people wrote, and can contain
instructions aimed at a model.

A `get_account_info` call also records the active workspace's name, which `/granola-status` shows, as a model's call
does.

## The export folder is outside the project

`export_markdown` writes under its export folder, which is normally outside the project directory (by default
`Granola` in your home folder). OpenCode asks for `external_directory` as well as the export's own action, so a rule for
`granola_export_markdown` alone is not enough in a run where nobody is present. Allow both, for instance:

```json
[
  { "action": "granola_export_markdown", "resource": "scheduled/*", "effect": "allow" },
  { "action": "external_directory", "resource": "<the export folder>/scheduled/*", "effect": "allow" }
]
```

A refusal that names `external_directory` costs nothing: nothing is read and nothing is written. Point the export folder
inside the project, or grant the rule, and call again.

## Errors

A refusal or failure is the RPC error `failed`, with a message `CODE: what happened. Next step: what to do.` and
`data: { code, next }`. `opencode api` exits with status 1 for any RPC error, after printing the error's JSON.

| Code | When |
| --- | --- |
| `PERMISSION_DENIED` | The rules ask or deny. An `ask` is refused before dispatch: the message says the action would ask, and the next step says to add an allow rule. A `deny` names the denied action, such as `granola_get_meetings`, and its next step says to remove or narrow that deny rule, add a later allow rule to the session, or use a session whose agent allows it. |
| `SESSION_UNKNOWN` | OpenCode says the session does not exist in this location. Any other failure to look the session up is OpenCode's own error. |
| `SESSION_AGENT_REQUIRED` | The session names no agent, or an agent that does not exist. |
| `TOOL_UNAVAILABLE` | The server is connected, but OpenCode does not list the tool, usually because your Granola plan does not include it. |
| `SERVER_CONFLICT` | Your OpenCode config defines its own `granola` server for another URL, which this plugin does not manage. |
| `AUTH_REQUIRED`, `CONNECTING`, `CONNECTION_FAILED`, `DISABLED`, `NOT_REGISTERED` | The `granola` server needs a sign-in, is still connecting (or reconnected while the call ran), could not connect, is disabled, or is missing. The next step is the one `/granola-status` gives, the same as the model gets. |
| `UPSTREAM_ERROR` | Granola answered with an error, such as a meeting that does not exist or a feature your plan does not include. The message holds the first line of Granola's text, at most 300 characters, with tokens and URL query strings removed. |
| `CANCELLED` | The request was cancelled. |

OpenCode itself answers `rpc.method_not_found` for a method that does not exist, such as a tool Granola adds later,
`rpc.unavailable` when the plugin did not register the tools RPC or the call reached another location, and
`rpc.invalid_input` for a body that is not the envelope above, with one message per problem.
`events_list` and `probe` also give the source contract's own codes, such as `INPUT_INVALID`, `CURSOR_INVALID`,
`ACCOUNT_MISMATCH` and `UNAVAILABLE`, with the next steps in the [configuration guide](configuration.md#events-list-1).


## What scripts cannot do

- Call a tool that Granola adds later, even with an allow rule, until this plugin classifies it.
- Call `sign_out`: it is not a method, and `opencode mcp logout granola` is how to revoke the grant.
- Run a write, a send or the export under a restricted `access`, or after you add a rule for it.
- Answer an approval prompt, or use a tool that asks.
- Use a token: the plugin has none to give.

A script's calls write nothing to the session, and OpenCode's `execute.before` and `execute.after` tool hooks, from any
plugin, do not run for them. The plugin applies its own hook's work itself: the workspace name and the connection
errors above.
